utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to say good morning to all the people in the courtroom, the accused, the Defence counsel, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, the other way round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and everybody else in the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, I give you the floor for the IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The OTP submitted a response to 2D objections regarding OTP exhibits tendered through Witness Rajkov. That shall be given Exhibit number IC 272. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness DA. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number 273. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 274, and the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 275. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Let's go into private session for a few moments, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session I think we have the first witness coming in this morning don't we, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. The Prosecution is prepared for the evidence of Omer Dilberovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us have the first witness shown in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I'm going to start off by checking whether you can hear what I'm saying in your own language. If so, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called as a Prosecution witness to testify here on the events that took place in the town of Mostar. I'm going to ask you to stand and take the solemn declaration. Can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth first, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Omer Dilberovic, and I was born on the 20th of September, 1945, in Orahovica, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I am not employed. I used to work before the conflict. I was a driver. But since then I have not been employed anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you ever testified before a court of law on the events that took place in your country or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you now go ahead and read the solemn declaration the usher is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some information from me to start off with. The Prosecution is going to begin by asking you questions and probably show you some documents. The Prosecutor has indicated that he needs about 30 minutes for that examination. After that first stage, the counsel sitting to your left, and although there are many of them, there is one who will be questioning you for each of the accused -- can also ask you questions. We envisage that the Defence will have one hour for their cross-examination if they need to, and they can distribute it amongst themselves as they see fit. Now, as there are 60 minutes in an hour and six accused, then theoretically, each of the Defence teams has 10 minutes. The three Judges sitting in front of you can also ask you questions at any time. I'm sure we'll be asking you about very specific matters if we consider that absolutely necessary. If you don't understand a question, then ask the person posing it to reformulate it, to ask it again. If you're feeling poorly at any time, just let us know. We're there to see that everything in the courtroom runs as smoothly as possible. That is what I wanted to inform you of as an introduction, and now without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution to start off with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dilberovic.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to begin by asking you some questions concerning a statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember giving such a statement in 2001?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that point in time, sir, did you answer the questions truthfully?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I answered them truthfully, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you answer the questions to the best of your recollection at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I do believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And upon the conclusion of that interview, was your statement read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you then sign an English language version of your written statement?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I signed an English language version of the statement. However, I was not able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask now, with the assistance of the usher, if the witness can be provided with a bundle of documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, as we're running under 92 ter procedure, perhaps you could give us a brief summary of the written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I neglected to do so, as my case manager also just pointed out to me. Let me read into the record the Rule 65 ter summary. Omer Dilberovic was a resident of East Mostar. His son was a member of the armija Bosnia and Herzegovina and was killed by a sniper on 13 June 1993. On 30 August 1993, the witness was on his way home from visiting his son's grave when he was shot in the leg by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, could you please turn to the document that has the tab 9854 in the bundle in front of you, please. 9854. Mr. Dilberovic, is P 09854 your written statement in the English language?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And does your signature appear on that document?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, if you could now turn several pages into that exhibit you'll find the Bosnian language version of your statement. It should be one more page, I believe. Mr. Dilberovic, when you arrived here in The Hague two days ago, did an investigator provide you with a Bosnian language copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to read and review that statement?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And yesterday afternoon when we met, did you make any corrections or changes to your written statement?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a small change, and it says that my son was hit on the 12th of June, 1993, whereas I attended my son's funeral. His mother didn't go or anybody else, I just did. I went home with two soldiers who brought me in when I wasn't feeling well and was semiconscious, and after that, on the 30th of August, 1993, I took my wife to the place where my son was buried so that she could see it. And another lady, Anita Kulak, also went. She lived next door, so she went with us. And that was on the 30th of August, and that's when I, myself, was wounded upon returning from the cemetery at Mazoljice. So that's just a small correction. I wasn't wounded when I went to my son's funeral but I was wounded on the 30th of August when I went to the cemetery again to take my wife and this other lady with me, and on the way back I was wounded at Mazoljice. So that's the correction I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you've made a couple of references to the 30th of August. What year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, there are a couple of additional items that I'd like to ask you about that aren't included in your witness statement, and so perhaps the best way for me to do that is simply to ask you what happened on the 30th of August, 1993, as you were returning from your son's grave. Can you briefly tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the place where my son was killed and buried in Osman Dzikic park in Mostar. I was there with my wife and my neighbour. Anita Kulak was her name. We were going back home when we had done what we came to do, and when we reached Mazoljice we had to pass through an old abandoned house, and there we had to run across an open space, and while we did that we heard sniper fire, sniper shots. They were coming, I don't know from where, but we felt that it was a sniper, and for a few minutes we stopped there until the shooting had calmed down. Then Anita Kulak and my wife rushed across the field. They ran across it and were able to come out the other side successfully. I waited for another minute and then I, too, quickly crossed the field. And when I came to the middle of the field and put out my right leg, the sniper hit me in my right leg and I fell to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there, Mr. Dilberovic. First of all, you indicated that "for a few minutes we stopped there until the shooting had calmed down." Where did you stop?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: In that same abandoned house. There was nobody there. And we all passed through that house and that's where we were. We stayed there for a couple of minutes because we had to go through the house to cross the field to reach the other house -- the other side where there was no longer any danger from that house to my house because there was shelter from the snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you told us that you were struck in the right leg. Can you tell us where on your right leg?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was hit in my right leg on the left side and the bullet came out by my right hip, and it just missed my hip by a few centimetres. That's what the doctors told me when I was in Zenica, in the hospital there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on which part of your right leg did the bullet enter?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: It entered through my thigh and exited by my right hip, the upper part of my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, now can you continue telling us what happened after you were struck by this bullet?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: When the bullet hit me, I saw Mrs. Anita and my wife moving towards me, but I said out loud to them, "Don't come near. I'm fine. Because the sniper's going to shoot at you, too, and might hit you." I heard them cry. I got up on my leg because I wanted to show them that I was all right. I was afraid that they would come towards me. I put out my left leg forward, left leg forward and then my right leg, and then my leg turned around because it was -- the hip bone had been fractured. And I couldn't walk. It was just limp. So I had to crawl to the yard. Before it was a garden, it was a nice garden, but now it's a yard between those two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, approximately what time this incident occurred on 30 August 1993?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of August, 1993, I did not have a watch so I didn't know the exact time, but I do know that it was afternoon, in the afternoon. We usually went that way early. If you wanted to cross that way you had to either go very early or late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us about the weather conditions on that day and the visibility on that day to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: On that day - I remember well - there was no precipitation, no rain, nothing. It was a nice day. No fog, no clouds, nothing. A very clear visible day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what were you wearing on that day, if you remember, Mr. Dilberovic?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I was wearing some blue trousers and a short jacket, a blue jacket, grey-blue, and I had some shoes on my feet. One -- one was left in the hospital and the other by that house, so I was left without any shoes in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, at the -- at the time when you and your wife and Anita Kulak were at this Mazoljice area, were there any other people around you?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody. We didn't see anybody then. When we passed through the house we were alone. And when I was hit, when he hit me, when I was in front of the house there were a lot of women who came to my assistance. They tried to bandage the wound, brought in some blankets and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time, Mr. Dilberovic, when you and your wife and Anita Kulak were at Mazoljice, was there any heavy equipment or machinery or military vehicles or anything of the like in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, nothing there. It was the suburbs, the outskirts of town, not too many houses there. It was all open space, quite visible. There were no soldiers. All you could see was a civilian run across that field going to their house or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, you mentioned a few moments ago that you heard some gunshots. Can you tell us a little bit more about the gunshots that you heard before you were shot?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You know that when a sniper fires he fires individual shots, and when we were in the house, we said we're going to wait a bit. We all agreed on that, because the sniper is firing and he would probably hit us. So we stayed there for some time waiting until it was quiet, until the sniper had stopped shooting. And when they crossed there was no shooting. However, when I stepped out and started running across, then you could hear this one bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the vicinity where you were at this abandoned house near Mazoljice, was there combat going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. There was a lull. It was quiet. There was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, did you hear the gunshot that actually struck you?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear the gunshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From which direction did you hear this gunshot?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: The gunshot came from -- well, on the eastern side of Mostar town, that's where I was, and the gunshot came from the west of Mostar because there couldn't have been anybody in front of me. There was an open space. No houses, just an open, clear space in front of me. So I came to the conclusion that that was it, that the bullet had come from the western side of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dilberovic, do you have any more specific information about where this bullet came from? Can you be more specific where in the west the bullet came from?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the area where I was crossing, in the eastern part of town, and that part is called Mazoljice. The bullet came from the western side, western direction, and I concluded -- that's what I concluded, that the bullet came from the western side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dilberovic, do you remember in 2004 meeting with an investigator and photographer of the Tribunal at Mazoljice?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I readily accepted to talk to them, at least to be able to tell somebody the truth, what happened to me and my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that point in time when you met the investigator and the photographer, they asked you a series of questions, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And those questions and answers were videotaped?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Probably they were videotaped, yes. They were filming something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, we would now like to show the witness P 09140 by way of Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dilberovic, if you could look at the screen in front of you please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "Investigator: Mr. Dilberovic, could you please indicate the open area where you were planning to cross. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. To the best of your recollection, could you please indicate the spot where you were shot at while running across this open area. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. Could you please indicate where you were hit. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. And to the best of your recollection, could you please point out the direction from where you heard the shot presumably coming from. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dilberovic, did you recognise yourself in that videotape?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see the video here, but I have viewed it. That was indeed what I said for that video, and the questions were as you heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you understood all those questions and answered them truthfully?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play that clip again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. I was actually going to do that, and if we could actually ask the witness, I would prefer to stop at the point where he indicates where he was hit, or we can play it through again and I can then take him back to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "Investigator: Mr. Dilberovic, could you please indicate the open area that you were planning to cross. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. To the best of your recollection, could you please indicate the spot where you were shot at while running across this open area. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. Could you please indicate where you were hit. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. And to the best of your recollection, could you please point out the direction from where you heard the shot presumably coming from. "Witness: [Indicates]"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to see this video again because I see a flagrant discrepancy between the area where he says he was shot and the area he pointed out as the area where the shooting came from. On the video, sir, you are showing your right leg and then you are showing to your left when you are asked where the shot came from. If the bullet comes from the right and hits your right leg, it goes through your right leg and exits your body. However, are you are showing on the video that you -- your right leg was hit by the bullet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's true. I was hit in my right leg. As I was running, I stretched out my right leg and the sniper hit me in that right leg, because the entry wound was quite clear. And the difference between an entry wound and an entry and exit wound is very distinct. I know that I was hit from the western part of town. I was on the east side. I stretch out my right leg. The bullet came like this, from that side, and it hit my right leg and then I fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, if we show it again I will ask Ms. Winner to stop the videotape and ask the witness some questions about precisely what it is he's pointing to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "Investigator: Mr. Dilberovic, could you please indicate the open area that you were planning to cross. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. To the best of your recollection could you please indicate the spot where you were shot at while running across this open area. "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Thank you. Could you please indicate where you were hit. "Witness: [Indicates]"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my right leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, with your left hand in this video, what are you pointing at with your left hand in this video?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm showing the point of entry of the bullet and the exit point was on the other side. That's what I was showing with my left hand when asked where I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what are you pointing to in the video with your right hand?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I was just holding my hand like that. In fact, where my right hand was is approximately the point where the bullet exited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So with your left hand you were showing the point of entry, and we see your left hand clearly on the video. At least that deserved to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we need to, we can run that segment of the videotape again in its entirety if that would be helpful. Would you -- no, not necessary? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, I'm now going to show you a panoramic 360-degree photograph, and I'm going to ask you some questions about this photograph, and I would ask you, sir, to tell me if you can spot anything that you see in the photograph. Mr. Dilberovic, do you recognise what you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: This is the area I was trying to cross in order to get to my house in Pasjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, we have captured three photographs from this -- this 360-degree photograph, and I'd ask that the witness be shown this so that he can mark the photograph and we can preserve it this way for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just for a moment. While we are here we need to correct the record. Page 16, line 18. The witness used the word running across, and the -- it was translated as crossing over. It will be important later because of speed when we hear the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If the usher could be of assistance, please, and -- and perhaps those could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, perhaps, Mr. Dilberovic, if you could look actually onto the photograph on your right.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Here is the road I was trying to run across.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you -- let me ask you this: In this photograph, is West Mostar visible?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the west side better than the east side because this is on an elevation, which makes West Mostar better visible than the east side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please take a marker that the usher will provide to you and circle or draw an oval around West Mostar as it's visible from this photograph.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I make a circle here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: And here. It was here in this direction approximately. This is the west side of the town of Mostar that I can see. Maybe it was even closer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just made three circles on three buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are silos. I know for sure, and I know that it's the west side of the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these are silos.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that for a fact. And I believe on the other side there are even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever cross that path before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in later hours when there was no shooting. It was calmer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you knew there was a sniper in ambush. According to you, where was he located, in which spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you precisely. I wouldn't know. I know that it came from the west side, but where he was shooting from and how, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether perhaps the witness could be invited to actually deal with precisely what Mr. Mundis asked him to do. It's entirely what the Prosecution asked, but once a question is asked, the witness ought to deal with it. He was asked to draw a circle around West Mostar and he hasn't done that. Well, an oval actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stewart, you're right. The question was broader, in more general terms. Witness, the Prosecutor asked you to make a circle on this photograph to indicate what you believed to be West Mostar. Instead, you made three circles, three little ones. Could you please draw a bigger circle to show us western Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the direction of these buildings. You see, I drew this broad line here. That side is the west side of town as far as I can -- from here to that point, that is part of the west side. And here where this car is is the east side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the west part of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see a yellow car here and then a line above it. Between the car and the line, at the time when you were hurt, when you were injured, were there any ABH units in the area between the line you drew and the yellow car?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting Your Honour's question, but the witness still has the pen. He indicated all sorts of things with his finger which then don't go on the record. I apologise, but I really do feel it's appropriate to press that he does do with the pen precisely what he was asked to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought he did answer your question, but maybe you didn't understand. He said that in his eyes, in his understanding, western Mostar was everything above that line, beyond that line. So behind the line is West Mostar. Now, I have a question. We have to know under whose control was the area between the line and the yellow car. To the best of your knowledge, were there any ABH units there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, up here there are not many houses, and this car was not there, nor was this -- any greenery in August, and this area was better visible than now, because you could see the road where the vehicle is standing in this picture. There was no car at that time, but the garage was there. There were no troops at all, because there were troops down there at the separation line holding the Santic Street in Mostar between the HVO and the army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could now look again, sir -- and perhaps the usher can just remain there because we'll go to the next photos in a moment. Sir, if you can look again at the screen in front of you, I'm going to move the photograph, and I'd ask you to tell us if you recognise anything that's visible in the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the house through which we passed coming from the lower side, coming out on the upper side and running across that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for technical reasons and in order to save time later, we have already moved to another photograph, but maybe we should get a number for the previous one rather than come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the previous photograph, are you going ask for an IC number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first photo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit IC 276.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm going to continue moving the photograph, Mr. Dilberovic.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: That is the building. There's nothing beyond. That's where we passed through to the clearing that I had to run across in order to get home. Not only myself, of course. All of us had to pass through there. All the civilians going in that direction had to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is -- Mr. Dilberovic, is this the house that you earlier told us was the abandoned house?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, we have a capture of this building, and I would ask you, sir, if you could please take a look at that to your right. And if you could please mark that -- mark the abandoned house where you with your wife and Ms. Kulak waited. If you could put an X on the abandoned house as you called it.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'd also ask that this be given an IC number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, if you now again look at the computer screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the building that was there. That's the track in the middle of which I was hit by a bullet. Yes, Your Honour. In that building across the road with a fence, that's something that did not exist at the time. All that was built later, including the greenery and the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dilberovic, we have a video still of this photograph as well, and I'd ask that be put on the ELMO next to you. Do you see the location -- do you see the location where your wife and Ms. -- Mrs. Kulak were at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. They were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could please mark that spot with an X.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, where did you go after you were shot, immediately after you were shot? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to hospital, the institute of hygiene in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. My question wasn't clear. Immediately after you were shot you told us you tried to get up and fell down. What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got here to where my wife and Ms. Anita were standing, here, the spot that I marked. I reached this place and then they hauled me from here to a place where some first aid was given to me, bandaging, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask, Mr. President, that this also be given an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dilberovic, you mentioned that you were taken to the hospital. I would ask you now, sir, if you could please take a look at what's in the bundle in front of you, 8404. Sir, can you tell us what this document P 08404 is?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: When I was in the hospital in Zenica where I was taken by helicopter from Mostar, I was hospitalised from the 8th of September, 1993, to the 21st of March, 1994, and here below you can see that I was injured on the 30th of August, 1993. It's the document from the hospital certifying that I was there for seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please turn, sir, to P 08756. Can you tell us what that document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: We went on mass at the North Camp when there were doctors who gave you an assessment for purposes of invalidity pensions, disability pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what is this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I was given this document which read 20 per cent disability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the last document I'd like to show you, sir, is 8170, P 08170.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Can't see it. 8170.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It should be the second document in the bundle. 8170. And can you tell us, sir, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I asked for this document because, we, who lost a family member, had the right to free treatment. We who lost somebody in the war were entitled to free treatment, so I asked for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to whom does this document refer?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: That's my son, Semir, born on the 15th of December, 1967. All this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in 1993, were you a civilian or were you a member of the armija?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was a civilian all the time, and everybody was registered somewhere, the civilian protection or somewhere, but since there was no need of me, nobody ever asked for me nor did I go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, we have no further questions for you. I'd like to thank you for coming to the Tribunal and testifying. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have two short questions for you. We have seen the photographs on which you left one building in order to go to another house where your wife and another lady were waiting for you. You were planning to run across that clearing. How many metres approximately?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot tell you exactly. I didn't measure, but approximately 20 metres. A metre less or more. I did not measure, but it was around 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the exact address of that spot where you were hit, you spoke of Mazoljice. Is that the name of the neighbourhood or the street or the spot?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Mazoljice; right. There were houses there. Somebody lived there. Mazoljice is a suburb, a street that runs through, and only 300 or 400 metres away is my neighbourhood called Pasjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a shame, Mr. Mundis, that we don't have a map, because he could have indicated the neighbourhood on the map. Registrar, can we see on our screens the famous map of Mostar? You don't have it. And the last question, sir. To your knowledge, at the place you were hit, wounded, before you, were there any people who were wounded or killed before you? And what about after you? To your knowledge, was anybody wounded or killed at the same spot after you?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard them shout out that it was a place you had to be careful because there was sniper fire and that there were a lot of people who had been wounded there, but I myself don't know who was wounded or what. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a moment ago you spoke about civilian protection, and my question is a follow-up question to what the President asked you. In the area that you were wounded, were there any members of the civilian protection or any armed persons or soldiers that were exchanging fire with West Mostar, which is where you say the bullet came from? Was there any exchange of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There was absolutely no shooting, but even if there had been, nobody could have shot from there because they would have been hit straight away from the western part. So if anything was done, if there was any shooting, it was in the town up at the separation lines, that is, Santic Street that I mentioned and places like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have the map on our screens in front of us. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you use a marker pen to indicate the spot you were wounded? You can put a cross or whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mazoljice is towards Pasjak, so that would be somewhere here. Hereabouts, towards Pasjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, there.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this is probably the road, and I was wounded somewhere around here. My house is here, and this is Mazoljice. So I was in between Mazoljice and the houses here crossing over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, on that same map, can you draw in the front line as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't really make my way on this map. I could give you the street names, but I can't find my way on this map, and I don't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. That will suffice. Mr. Registrar, give us an IC number for the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have half an hour before the break, so let's start off with the cross-examination, and which Defence team is going to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Praljak will be the first team. I have a few questions for the witness, and I think they will help clarify some location issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise for not being able to address you with your name. Oh, yes, I can. I apologise. You weren't given a pseudonym. You are Mr. Dilberovic.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions and additional explanations that I would like to hear from you. Let's go back to the question of location. You showed us the spot that you were wounded at, and the position is somewhere between Mazoljice and Pasjak, as you said. So that's a micro-area, this little cul-de-sac, little road, path. Does it have another name?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: It was private property. It was probably private property, and there was - what shall I call it? A field, a valley where there wasn't a path, but there's a path there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And may I ask you to give me yes or no answers if that is possible without additional explanations because we simply don't have time. So your answer was it doesn't have any name. This path hasn't got a name.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of any name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you said that it was a nice day and that the incident occurred sometime in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the date, it must have been very hot.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It wasn't too hot, because it was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But we're talking about the 30th of August, are we?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the 30th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you say it wasn't hot?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Not then, no. Not at that time. I didn't find it hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it humid and was there any wind?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said you ran across the clearing, and you showed us that and we saw a picture of it on our screens. Can you explain to us, please, the word "run across," "pretrcavati", that can mean walking fast, running slowly, or running fast. Which was it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I ran fast, faster than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you ran as fast as you could?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at my age, perhaps, it wasn't, objectively speaking, terribly fast, but I ran as fast as I could for my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. According to your age.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I ran the best I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly? You ran as fast as you could, as much as you could?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Probably out of fear I ran as fast as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. May we have on our screens the previous image, IC 276. And you'll see the photograph that you marked again, the three high-rise buildings on the western side which are referred to as the silos. Now, from the position you were at a little above the yellow van to the line that you drew in, that is the area controlled by the BH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am certain that that's the line. Maybe it's a little closer, but at least that was the furthest point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Slowly. Let's take it step-by-step. So from the place you were standing, how far is it to the Neretva River, 100 metres, 200, 500, roughly?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean where I live?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, where you were standing, where this photograph was taken from?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know how far it was, whether it was 1 kilometre or a kilometre and a half, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course you don't know exactly. That's fine. Just a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you said it might be one to one and a half kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us also in your rough estimate how far it is from the Neretva to the separation line between the HVO and the BH army? You mentioned Santica Street. So how far from Neretva to Santiceva street?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: 200, 300 metres. Santica street isn't too far from the Neretva River but I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I never measured the distance, nor did I give it much thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be sufficient. Now, you said today here when asked about the clothing you were wearing and for the transcript, you said you were wearing blue trousers and a blue jacket of some sort.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a bluey-grey. Whether you'd call it a grey jacket or blue jacket. Anyway, it was from some artificial material, fibre, sort of plasticy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In that statement that my learned friend of the Prosecution showed you to begin with, you said, "When I was wounded, I was wearing grey trousers which they later cut through, and I had a greyish jacket." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, grey or -- I'm not very good at colours. It was either sort of grey or blue or grey-blue. It wasn't white. It wasn't yellow anyway, that's for sure, but it was sort of grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, the jacket you have on now, Witness, what colour would you say that was?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's got several colours. I'd say black, dark. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the record, can we state that the witness is wearing an anthracite, dark grey jacket with lighter grey details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But we can agree, it's something you called blue-grey.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. If it was blue, it was blue. If it was grey, it was grey. But it was probably what I said in my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. In your first statement, you said you were wearing a grey jacket and grey trousers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably yes, because I remembered better at that time than I remember now after so much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in a word, because the Defence is taking a lot of time and I'm going to go to the heart of the matter. What you were wearing, what you were wearing, could it be compared to any type of military uniform, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, not at all. It didn't resemble any kind of army uniform. No, it did not. It didn't resemble any kind of military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I think you said that you heard the shot.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So now I'd like to ask you this: You know that when a firearm or, let's say, a rifle shoots, you hear the sound of the explosion at the place in which it is detonated. That is to say at the rifle spot.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you know that there is the sound of the projectile as well, the bullet? That makes a sound too.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: We didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that what you heard was the sound that you heard when a bullet was being fired, is fired?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that you could then have heard the bullet firing at a distance of at least one kilometre and several metres from the place you were hit?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I heard the shot being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The firing.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard the shot being fired when the bullet hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. You described to us and we saw it on the video as well -- you showed us the direction from which you consider that the bullet had come, and you indicated that it was from the west side.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you be more precise and say where from the west? To the far left, from the centre, to the far right?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you have the road or path here, then the west is in the direction of the road, the western part of town. It's neither left nor right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you say that it's a continuation of the direction of this path?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that part of town over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it's a direction.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's that direction in that part of town, because this officially was the eastern side of town and over there was the western side of town. So if you followed the direction of the path, you would get to the western side of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you describe the western side, you first made circles round these three high-rise buildings that you called the silos. So those buildings are to the right of the path?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you drew circles round those high-rise buildings, do you think that the projectile could have come from those high-rise buildings?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No. The gentleman asked me where the western side of town was, and I said, to be quite certain, from the silos that way. I said that it could be closer, but I know exactly what I drew here, and that is exactly in the western part of town. That's why I took the silos as a demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, to conclude, you can't be more precise than say that it was from the western side of town?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can't say anything else because there were no houses in front of where I was hit for me to have any doubts that the bullet could have come from somewhere else. So that's why I said that, what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any more questions. I think General Praljak might, though. Thank you, Witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dilberovic.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'd like the usher's assistance to place a document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the 12th of June when you attended your son's funeral in the cemetery, from that place, the cemetery, can you see Hum hill? Can you see Hum well?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You can't see it well?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, you can't, because it -- there are buildings in the way, and it's in the middle of town, in the eastern part where Osman Dzikic's monument is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, on this photograph. I think the expert put a 6 on this image, on the map. Is that the place you were hit, where the number 6 is?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I can't find my way here at all. I can't orientate myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Mazoljice is?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's where I was hit and wounded but I can't say anything precise on the map because I'm afraid of making a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you see the area to the left of 6 -- of -- 6, yes. Do we agree that that's the railway station and that there's a long road called Marsal Tito Street running that way, the one parallel to the Neretva River, running parallel. We have the Carinski bridge and then we have the railroad station and below the railroad station we have Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Everything you're saying is quite right, but I just can't find my way on this map here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Look underneath that number 6. Do you remember where the war hospital was of the BH army below you, in that general area.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the institute of hygiene?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Show me where the institute of hygiene is then?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I've already said I can tell you all this orally but I can't find my way on the map. I don't know. I really can't make it out on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, I understand you completely. So underneath -- below you somewhere was the institute of hygiene; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can say what I know but I can't do anything better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that above the institute of hygiene there is a little hill towards you?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that just below that hill there were positions of mortars of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no mortars there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that something you know or something that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I know there were troops, but I don't know about mortars. Maybe there were mortars. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you're not sure whether there were mortars or not.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you know that there were troops there?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were troops around the institute of hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you for answering these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Dilberovic, did you go the same way when you went to visit your son's grave?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that was early in the afternoon, was it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You told the Court earlier and said in your statement that you usually went either very early in the day or very late. Why did you choose to go more in the middle of the day on the first occasion, as you told the Court, that you were taking your wife to go to visit your son's grave given that is was, according to you, more dangerous to go then?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My wife had not been to our son's grave for two months. She decided to either go or die. I wanted to wait until late afternoon, but she didn't want to wait. She would have gone alone if I hadn't accompanied her. That's why I had to go at that hour, that time, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you take similar precautions on the way to cross this particular open space?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we were going there from our house, we did the same. The sniper was not shooting. We didn't even hear him anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any shooting going on when you went?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Only when I climbed down towards the cemetery we could hear shells, but further away from the town, whether it was in Nevesinje -- and shells were falling from both sides probably, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, on the way back then -- first of all, let's get clear. You said in your statement, paragraph 19, that you waited half an hour before crossing this space. This morning you said it was a few minutes. Now, was it -- was it quite a long time, like half an hour that you waited or was it a very short time? Can we be clear.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I did not have a watch. I cannot tell you whether it was half an hour or less. I don't know that for sure. I just waited for the shooting to stop. That's the main thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: For how long, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's proceed on, then. And also it's quite clear from your recollection now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Mr. Stewart is asking an important question that I wanted to ask myself. It struck me that you said you'd waited half an hour. If you had waited half an hour, then it must have been because you had heard shooting, and you told yourself, "I can perhaps avoid that," and you waited for around half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. I heard shooting. And only when the shooting stopped I ran across, when I could no longer hear the shooting from that sniper or other weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we to conclude that during that half hour you heard one or more than one sniper who was shooting everywhere, or were they shooting precisely at the spot where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the shooting stopped and when I was hit by that bullet, I no longer heard the sniper. I was there for a while, and some people hauled me back the same way, and the sniper wasn't shooting any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You -- just to clear something up. You said in your statement that your wife and your neighbour Anita walked and didn't run. You said this morning that they ran across. Again, as clearly as you can remember, was it true that they ran?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: They probably ran. I can't remember. But whenever you come across a space, a spot that is dangerous, people run across.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. All right. You can't remember. [Microphone not activated] Now, when you said in your statement --

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember about that, but I did run.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's move on then. You said in your statement that you waited for about half an hour. We could still here some shooting but they were not so often. So the position is this, isn't it, there was no shooting worth mentioning on the way to the cemetery in the morning. On the way back, there was a lot of shooting going on, so you waited and then when the shooting was a bit less, you decided that you were going to have to risk it so that your wife and Anita first and then you ran across the space. That's what happened, isn't?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you were very unfortunate. You were hit. Just want to be clear. The way you described the wound this morning made it sound as if the exit, you understand what I mean by the exit wound, that where the bullet came out, it sounded as if it was even slightly higher than where it went in. Is that -- is that right? That's the way it sounded this morning.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The exit wound is smaller, and the entry wound is bigger than the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not concerned about the size, but I just want to confirm with you the way you made it sound was the exit wound was higher up. It was nearer to your hip. That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: The exit wound is not above the hip. It's below the hip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: If it had been above, it would have destroyed my hip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The exit wound is slightly higher than the entry wound?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: The exit wound is bigger than the entry wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got lots of questions. I do wish -- not lots. I have a few minutes. I wish to press this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we be very clear, Witness. Perhaps you could even just stand up for us. I'm sorry to have to ask you to do this but we need to get this clear. Just stand up for us and mark with your finger where the bullet went into your leg and just mark it just very clearly, particularly so the Judges can see. That's terribly important.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I can explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: That's where the building was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I will. I will tell you. I just moved to make a step. The bullet hit me here. I still have a scar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where did it come out?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: And it came here below the hip. And the wound here was bigger than the entry wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Next question -- sorry. Can we -- I'm grateful for suggestions, but I'd prefer not to cross-examine by committee. All right? Please. We'll come back to it. When you were on the ground crawling, you don't describe -- there was no attempt to shoot you then, was there?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- so you -- you managed safely -- how long did it take you? From when you were shot and on the ground crawling to when you were able to get out of -- under cover, out of the open, how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: You know what? I started immediately wanting to run but I couldn't, and then I got crawling to the gate. I don't know how long it took me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, was it -- it must have been two minutes or something like that minimum, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. You can try to infer. It was about 20 metres. I was hit in the middle. How long it could have taken me to crawl. I don't know the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's put it this way: If there was a sniper and he had been deliberately shooting at you, he had plenty of time to shoot you again, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: When they hit a person, they usually wait for other people --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: -- to come --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: -- hit them and try to kill them. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to shoot you he would have had plenty of time to do it, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the hospital, you said originally in your statement that the doctor told you you were the 53rd person to be shot by a sniper that day. Now, you've changed that as a result of the proofing, and you now say the doctor told you that you were the 53rd person to be wounded that day. So it's very clear. It was -- it became a very busy day as far as shooting was concerned, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me to say this. When I got to the institute of hygiene, to the hospital, I was in great pain, because probably when I tried to run I hurt my leg any more and I was in great pain. They gave me first aid. I wasn't bleeding any more. And then the doctor approached and I asked him, "Doctor, please, give me an injection or something. I can't stand this pain any more." And he said, "Be quiet. You see how many of them there are here. You are going to be fine."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: And the doctor said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't want to press you further about what happened at the hospital then. We've got an answer to that. Now, on this busy day, something that you don't mention but which the Dutch expert mentions, lieutenant Van Der Weijden, he says and you are clearly the source of this, it's page 20 of his report, he specifically records that you stopped for an instant at a location marked X which is pretty much the point you were shot for a peek towards the front line. Now, you must be the source of that information. That's correct, is it, that as you were crossing that open space, you stopped or you say you were running, but you stopped and had a look towards the front line. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that was --

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. When a bullet hits you, you are probably going to turn around and look where it came from, but I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was a lot going on, and you looked towards the front line because there was a lot of activity at that time in the afternoon, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: OMER DILBEROVIC
utterances.text: It could be. It could be right that I looked at the lower side to see where it came from, but I can't remember whether I looked or not or I just fell. I could easily have looked. But what is there to look at? I just fell immediately as I was hit. It fell me to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two short linked questions. I know Mr. Petkovic may want to ask something, Your Honour, but it's this. First of all, Your Honour, it's suggested and I do -- I do accept my learned friend's suggestions, we should put this on the record, that a description, because we all saw it of what the witness said of the entry and exit wound, I hope Your Honours will agree that the witness pointed to places for the entry wound and place for the exit wound which made it clear as we saw in court that the exit wound was slightly higher than the entry wound. I hope Your Honours will agree for the record that that was what the witness indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that point we can question the expert or a doctor, but you know as well as I do that sometimes a bullet enters the body and as a result of resistance it encounters, it can go higher or lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can have that confirmed later --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm only asking to have it made absolutely clear for the record what this witness's evidence was on that point and then what questions arise in the future are another matter. Your Honour, if there is any doubt at all -- I'm seeking Your Honours confirmation that is what Your Honours saw this witness indicate. If not, we'll have to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Of course I'm not an expert on sniping, but I would like to say the following: According to this picture which we have seen and where the witness has made the sign where in his view the front line was in a way put between West and East Mostar, as far as my calculation and as I see it, this part of -- of Mostar west was a bit lower than this hill. We have here a hill in my view, and that's why the shot came from a bit below.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with -- with -- with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Then the wound from the exit wound was in a way a bit higher than -- than the -- than the one when it entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour I -- did I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: But I believe it is not a major question but my reading of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I was deliberately not entering into -- I'm not at this moment taking up what Your Honour says at all. I'm leaving that. But I'm not entering into either argument or more extensive evidence. My point is an extremely narrow one. It is just that this witness's evidence over about one minute on that particular point is -- is simply confirmed for the record as having been given in the terms in which it is given for what in the end it turns out to be worth. That's all, Your Honour. I've got to say, Your Honour, for the record, I am going to say that I saw the witness indicate very clearly that the exit wound was higher than the entry wound. I believe that my colleagues to whom I apologise for my testiness a few minutes ago, I believe that my colleagues saw exactly the same thing. I see nods from the committee which contribution I welcome this time. I see nods from that committee. If the Prosecution saw anything different they better re-examine on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you agree with what counsel just said? Counsel just said that the entry wound, the point where the bullet entered, is lower than the point where the bullet exited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the wound where the bullet entered, that's what I was trying to say, the entry wound is smaller than the exit wound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we are not talking about the size. Everybody knows that entry is always smaller than the exit. It's not the size. We're talking about the level, the height.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I had understood earlier. I thought the size was in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking to you about the level, about the height. Was the entry point lower than the exit point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I thought the size of the wound. It was bigger on this side than the entry wound, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we seem to be still in confusion about size and position. Your Honour, I'm reluctant to suggest this but we -- we feel there is a need in the circumstances. The witness of course unhappily still bears the scars as he made clear. Of course he knows where on his own leg and thigh these wounds are. Your Honour, could we invite him very quickly to just put his finger on exactly where the entry wound is and put his finger then exactly where the exit wound is and Your Honours can see it. Your Honours, I'm asking through Your Honours if the witness could be troubled to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stand up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness can be troubled to come where we can all see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hit here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stand in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please stand in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hit here, and that's where the bullet entered and left my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where my hip is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sometimes we work in inches, sometimes we work in centimetres, but it seems very clear that the -- where the witness is showing the exit wound is at least two or three centimetres higher than the entry wound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My metric colleagues will confirm that probably. I'm glad we got that sorted out. I'll allow the witness to put his headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My linked question is this, Witness: You appear to have been given some compensation on the basis of military disability. Can you reconcile how you came to be awarded something on the basis of military disability with your contention that you were throughout and at the time of this injury a civilian?
